method: The body-mass change method compares body mass immediately before and after a session. Every kilogram of mass lost is treated as approximately one litre of fluid, because one litre of sweat weighs close to one kilogram; the drink taken on during the session is added back and any urine passed is taken off, so sweat volume = (pre weight - post weight) + fluid drunk - urine passed. Dividing that volume by the session length in hours gives the hourly rate. Imperial input converts pounds to grams with the exact factor 453.59237 and US fluid ounces to millilitres with 29.5735295625 before the same arithmetic, so both unit systems agree. Percent body-mass change is the mass difference relative to the pre-exercise weight, shown from the before to the after weigh-in, so losing a kilogram reads -1 kg and finishing heavier reads positive. A session that implies zero or negative sweat loss is rejected rather than shown as a rate, because the inputs cannot support an estimate. Weights are bounded to 20-400 kg or 44-880 lb, fluids to 10 L or 340 fl oz, urine to 5 L or 170 fl oz, and sessions to whole minutes from 1 to 1440; every input accepts at most two decimal places and exponent notation is rejected rather than parsed. The tool assumes the two weigh-ins used the same scale and similar clothing, does not model evaporation, sodium or electrolyte losses, and gives no medical or hydration prescription; individual sweat rates vary widely and one session is only a sample. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand, Exercise and Fluid Replacement: sweat loss is estimated from body-mass change plus fluid consumed minus urine output.
Baker LB, Sweat rate and fluid balance research: the body-mass change method treats 1 kg of mass loss as approximately 1 L of sweat.
Sawka MN et al., Human water needs: sweat rates commonly fall near 0.5 to 2.0 L per hour, with large individual and environmental variation.
National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health heat-stress guidance: weighing a worker before and after a shift is a standard way to measure fluid loss.
